```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Time to a first paying customer fits the 90-day window better. A is a thin Stripe-webhook-to-fulfillment wrapper built on outsourced warehousing and printing, with no licensing gate. B needs IRS Authorized e-file Provider approval, which the brief says can take up to 45 days and includes fingerprinting, before a full filing product can go live.",
    "A carries much lower downside risk for a one-person, AI-run company. B's domain is high-stakes: per the brief, PFIC, FBAR and FATCA errors can cost customers tens of thousands of dollars. That creates liability and trust hurdles a new solo brand is poorly placed to clear against incumbents with 100k to 165k users.",
    "A's demand evidence is closer to proof of payment. The named SaaS companies (Endcrawl, BurnRate, Hampton) actually bought and used swag or automated welcome-box solutions. B's quotes show pain but no willingness to pay a new entrant.",
    "A's buyer is a SaaS company with a sourced pricing anchor (SwagUp at $99 to $999/mo plus fees). It can be sold one-to-one to founders without mass-market trust, and more than one customer relationship can come from direct outreach. B depends on individuals trusting an unknown tool with their tax filings.",
    "Both ideas face entrenched competitors with the same core offering. A's lack of a wedge is serious, since SwagUp and Zapier already do the exact mechanic. But B pairs the same competitive problem with regulatory and liability barriers, so A is still the more achievable first bet."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's demand evidence is three forum complaints about PFIC and FATCA confusion. None shows a DIY expat unhappy with Expatfile or MyExpatTaxes, or willing to switch to a new tool. The '$50K' quote concerns attorney and remediation liability, not software spend. The low-CAC channel claim rests on Expatfile's own referral payout, not a cost a new entrant has shown it can achieve, and the community-channel cost is explicitly marked as not found.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-low confidence. Both briefs describe crowded markets with incumbents already offering the core product, and neither identifies a proven wedge. A's own brief admits the Stripe-trigger mechanic is not a market gap. The decision rests mainly on B's documented regulatory delay and liability risk against the 90-day, one-person constraint, not on strong positive evidence for A."
}
```
